title: Fresh Pineapple Upside-Down Cake
changes_from_base: Fresh pineapple on a cooked brown-sugar caramel, and pineapple juice instead of milk in the batter; about 5 minutes longer.
summary: This follows the classic upside-down method, but swaps in fresh pineapple over a cooked brown-sugar caramel and uses pineapple juice instead of milk in the batter, with about 5 minutes extra in the oven.
equipment: 23 cm round cake tin (5 cm deep, not loose-based), base-lined and greased
stand mixer or electric hand whisk
serving plate larger than the tin

ingredients.item: fresh pineapple, peeled, cored and cut into 1 cm rings or half-moons
glacé cherries (naturally coloured) or pitted fresh cherries
fine sea salt or table salt, or table salt
cake flour (or plain flour; see note)
ingredients.note: plain flour works with a slightly firmer crumb

steps.title: Preheat the oven
steps.text: Heat the oven to 175°C (155°C fan) with a shelf in the middle, allowing at least 20 minutes for it to reach full temperature before the cake goes in. A properly heated oven helps the sponge rise evenly from the start rather than spreading before it sets.

steps.title: Cook the caramel
steps.text: Simmer the melted butter and brown sugar together in a small pan for 2 minutes, until thick and bubbling, then pour it into the tin. Lay the fresh pineapple over it in a single layer, tucking cherries into the gaps. Because fresh pineapple is juicier than tinned, cooking the caramel first thickens it enough to hold firm underneath the fruit.

steps.title: Cream the butter and sugar
steps.text: Beat the butter, caster sugar and salt for 3-4 minutes until pale and fluffy. Beat in the eggs one at a time, then mix in the vanilla extract. This builds the air structure that gives the sponge its rise.

steps.title: Fold in flour and pineapple juice
steps.text: On low speed, add the flour and baking powder in two additions, alternating with the pineapple juice, mixing just until smooth. Stop as soon as the flour disappears, since overmixing at this stage can make the crumb dense rather than light.

steps.title: Spoon batter over the fruit
steps.text: Spoon the batter over the pineapple in dollops, then spread it gently to the edges without disturbing the fruit underneath. Keeping a light hand here means the fruit stays exactly where you arranged it.

steps.title: Bake until set
steps.text: Bake for 45-50 minutes, a little longer than the classic version, until golden and springy with a skewer coming out clean from the centre. Fresh pineapple holds more moisture than tinned, so the extra few minutes let the middle fully set.

steps.title: Cool for exactly 10 minutes
steps.text: Leave the cake in the tin for exactly 10 minutes. The caramel is still warm and loose at this point, which allows the fruit to let go cleanly; any longer and it sets hard against the tin.

steps.title: Turn out and serve
steps.text: Run a knife around the edge, place a serving plate larger than the tin on top, and flip the cake over in one confident movement. Lift off the tin and press back any fruit that's stuck behind, then serve warm or at room temperature.

tips: Cook the caramel until it's thick and bubbling before adding the fruit, or the extra moisture from fresh pineapple can leave it watery.
Cut the fresh pineapple into even pieces so it releases moisture at a consistent rate and the top bakes level.
Resist turning the cake out before the 10 minutes are up, or the fruit can stick to the tin instead of releasing into the caramel.
Make sure the eggs are at room temperature so the batter mixes smoothly and rises evenly in the oven.
Don't taste the raw dough or batter: raw flour and raw egg aren't safe to eat until baked.
storage: Keep covered at room temperature for up to 1 day, or in the fridge for up to 3 days. Wrapped slices freeze for up to 2 months; thaw at room temperature and warm gently until just heated through before serving.
